articles.title: Here are Elon Musk’s wildest predictions about Tesla’s self-driving cars
articles.summary: Tesla CEO Elon Musk made a series of bold predictions today about the ability for his company’s cars to completely drive themselves. The comments, made at an invitation-only event, laid out a near-future vision in which self-driving Teslas vehicles compete with the likes of Waymo, GM, and Uber.
articles.body: Tesla CEO Elon Musk made a series of bold predictions today about the ability for his company’s cars to completely drive themselves. And Musk thinks it will happen sooner than most of his competitors — perhaps as soon as the end of this year. Musk made the comments at an invitation-only event for investors at Tesla’s Palo Alto-headquarters, laying out a near-future vision in which self-driving Teslas vehicles compete with the likes of Waymo, GM, and Uber. Here are some of the main takeaways from Tesla’s “autonomy day” event: * Tesla unveiled a new microchip that Musk said was being included in every new Tesla produced today. He called “the best chip in the world… objectively.” * It’s a high-performance, special-purpose chip built by Samsung in Texas, manufactured with autonomy and safety in mind. * The company is about halfway through the design process for the next-generation chip, which Musk estimated would be about three times better than the current system. * Musk estimated that by the middle of 2020, Tesla’s autonomous system will have improved to the point where drivers will not have to pay attention to the road. * He said the company will roll out autonomous taxis next year in some parts of the US. The service will allow Tesla owners to add their cars to a Tesla network, which he said would be akin to Uber or Airbnb. * “We will have more than one million robotaxis on the road,” Musk said. “A year from now, we’ll have over a million cars with full self-driving, software... everything.” * These cars will be Level 5 autonomy with no geofence, which is a fancy way of saying they will be capable of driving themselves anywhere on the planet, under all possible conditions, with no limitations. There are no cars on the road today that are Level 5. * Tesla robotaxis could generate owners up to $30,000 a year in profit, Musk predicted. * Musk promised that Tesla would soon be making cars that could last for at least one million miles, while requiring minimal maintenance. [Media: Musk has been criticized for overstating the autonomous capabilities of Tesla’s vehicles, while also beta testing semi-autonomous features on his customers — with occasional dire consequences. Teslas have been involved in a handful of crashes, some of them fatal, involving the use of the company’s Autopilot system. Musk is known for setting deadlines he cannot meet, and for making predictions that fail to come true. (Musk had previously forecast that his cars would be fully self-driving by 2018.) As a a result, his company’s stock is some of the most shorted in the world. But Musk saw the investor day as an opportunity to lay out in full his company’s bold plans for self-driving cars, while drawing a clear distinction between Tesla and every other company working on this technology today. It was a shot across the bow of an industry that has been taking pains recently to dial back expectations about the eventual rollout of self-driving cars. “The fundamental message consumers should be taking today is that it’s financially insane to buy anything other than a Tesla,” Musk said. “It’ll be like owning a horse in three years. I mean, fine if you want to own a horse, but you should go into it with that expectation.” [Image: Early reactions to Tesla’s dense presentation was positive, if skeptical. The company’s claims about the capability of its AI chip were noteworthy, and should have competitors like Nvidia and Intel-owned Mobileye nervous, says Sam Abuelsamid, senior analyst at Navigant. “Assuming that the new custom silicon actually lives up to the claims, the computer looks very impressive on a performance level,” Abuelsamid says. “This potentially puts them well ahead of what Nvidia and Intel/Mobileye are able to achieve right now at comparable power consumption levels. The only current compute platform that can exceed the Tesla claims is the Nvidia Pegasus, which consumes significantly more power.” Others were less impressed. Partners for Automated Vehicle Education, a coalition of autonomous vehicle industry players and nonprofits aimed at improving the public’s understanding of automated vehicles, posted a thread on Twitter during the presentation that criticized Musk’s claims without mentioning him by name. “It is damaging to public discussion about advanced vehicle technologies — and potentially unsafe — to refer to vehicles now available for sale to the public using inaccurate terms,” PAVE wrote. [Media: Tesla currently sells a “Full Self Driving” (FSD) option for $5,000 (or $7,000 after delivery), with Tesla’s recently unveiled “Navigate on Autopilot” feature that guides the car from “on-ramp to off-ramp” by suggesting and making lane changes, navigating highway interchanges, and proactively taking exits. The company recently pushed an over-the-air software update to enable automatic lane changes without any input from the driver. And later this year, Tesla promises that cars equipped with FSD will be able to drive automatically in cities, and “recognize and respond to traffic lights and stop signs.” The name “Full Self Driving” is just branding, and experts warn it is not representative of the car’s real capabilities. When activating Navigate on Autopilot, a warning screen pops up on the center display that reads, “Navigate on Autopilot does not make your Model 3 autonomous. Like other Autopilot features, the driver is still responsible for the car at all times.” Drivers who take their hands off the steering wheel risk disengaging the feature. Musk’s comments today have the potential to further muddy the waters with respect to how self-driving cars are discussed in public. Musk says Tesla’s vehicles have all the hardware necessary to enable “Full Self Driving.” That includes a sophisticated onboard computer, eight cameras that cover 360 degrees, front-facing radar, and short-range ultrasonic sensors. Pending regulatory approval, all Tesla needs to do is “flip the switch” and push a software update to transform an estimated 400,000 vehicles on the road today into self-driving cars. The company is said to be making progress on a new Autopilot neural net in its latest software update, but the idea that current regulations are preventing its rollout is confusing. There are no laws preventing Tesla from following through on this promise right now. As long as Tesla’s cars meet the current Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards — and they do — this can be accomplished whenever Musk wants. Most experts say that fully autonomous cars are still 10 years away, or even unachievable with Tesla’s vision-based approach. Nearly every company currently working on self-driving vehicles, including leaders like Alphabet’s Waymo, GM, and Ford, use a light-beam sensor called LIDAR. Musk calls LIDAR “a crutch,” and has long argued that it is too expensive and bulky for Tesla’s vehicles. At today’s event, Musk went further than he ever has in bashing companies that use laser sensors. “LIDAR is a fool’s errand, and anyone who relies on LIDAR is doomed,” he said. Companies that use LIDAR are adamant the sensor is a necessary ingredient for self-driving cars. “Vehicles that don’t have LIDAR, that don’t have advanced radar, that haven’t captured a 3D map are not self-driving vehicles,” Ken Washington, Ford’s chief technical officer, said during a recent interview with Recode. “They are great consumer vehicles with really good driver-assist technology.” Musk’s claims about the Tesla Network drew a lot of questions from investors about per-mile costs and liability. Asked who would be liable in the event of a crash involving a Tesla robotaxi, Musk said “probably Tesla.” Musk has been kicking around the idea of launching an Uber competitor for almost three years now. In 2016, Musk released his “Master Plan - Part Deux,” in which he proposed allowing Tesla owners to add their car to a “Tesla shared fleet,” which later become known as the “Tesla Network.” Musk described the network as an on-demand ride-hailing service in which Tesla owners can lend their vehicles for autonomous taxi rides when they’re at work or on vacation. Musk theorized that if used enough, the vehicle could potentially end up paying for itself. The idea fell off the radar for several years, as Tesla slipped into its Model 3 “production hell.” It resurfaced late last year, when Musk brought up the idea of renting out your Tesla vehicle like you would your home on Airbnb during an earnings call. “The advantage that Tesla will have is that we’ll have millions of cars in the field with full autonomy capability and no one else will have that,” he said at the time. “So I think that will end up putting us in the strongest competitive position long-term.” [Image: At Monday’s event, Musk offered his most detailed description of the robotaxi service, indicating the current cost would be $0.18 per mile and would decrease over time. While investors and experts process Tesla’s presentation, many critics warn that Musk’s statements should be taken with a grain of salt — especially as it relates to full autonomy. “Claiming that the Tesla cars have the hardware for full autonomy and only need the software is like saying that we have seeds, we just need to plow, plant, nurture, harvest and then eat,” said Raj Rajkumar, an electrical engineer at Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute. “Basically they are at the starting point — full autonomy is many years away.”

articles.title: DJI’s Mic 3 crams more features into a smaller package
articles.summary: DJI’s Mic 3 wireless lavalier microphone system is even smaller without scrimping on features or battery life.
articles.body: DJI is making its latest wireless lavalier microphone system even smaller without scrimping on features or battery life. The DJI Mic 3 is half the size and weight of its Mic 2 predecessor and introduces new capabilities, including two adaptive gain control modes, three voice tone presets, and a sizable increase in storage capacity for internal recordings. Pricing for the Mic 3 starts at $219 for one receiver and transmitter, or $329 for a kit containing two transmitters, a receiver, and the charging case. DJI says it won’t be available in the US immediately, however, and it’s currently showing as “out of stock” on DJI’s US webstore with no information regarding future availability. By comparison, the two-transmitter kit for the Mic 2 launched at $219, and the more affordable Mic Mini is $169, which makes this a pricey upgrade. DJI’s latest wireless mic can support up to four transmitters and eight receivers at once for recording audio from large groups, with a range of 400 meters (1,312 feet). The Mic 3 automatically switches between 2.4GHz and 5GHz frequency bands to help keep the transmission stable and prevent interference. Two-level active noise cancelling is also available for reducing background sounds. [Image: If you dislike the lack of a screen on DJI’s Mic Mini, the new Mic 3 looks like a good compact alternative. The Adaptive Gain Control modes include an Automatic option that can suppress sudden volume spikes and prevent clipping in noisy environments, and a Dynamic mode that automatically adjusts gain to keep volume consistent in quieter indoor settings like studios. The three voice tone presets include Regular, Rich, and Bright, which can be selected based on the vocal characteristics of whoever is speaking to adjust clarity. At 16 grams, the Mic 3 is closer in size and weight to the 10-gram Mic Mini system that DJI launched last year. Unlike the Mic Mini, however, the Mic 3 retains features like built-in backup recording abilities to prevent losing audio, and a touchscreen display on the receiver to adjust settings and monitor battery levels. It also includes 32GB of storage for dual-file internal recordings that support both 24-bit and 32-bit floating points, which is significantly larger than the 8GB of built-in storage on the Mic 2. Battery life sits between the two older DJI lav mics, providing up to eight hours for the receiver and 10 hours for the transmitter, compared to six hours for both on the Mic 2, and up to 11.5 hours and 10.5 hours on the Mic Mini’s transmitter and receiver, respectively. The Mic 3 charging case provides 2.4 full charges, according to DJI, giving users 28 hours of extra juice on the go. Update, August 29th: Added pricing information, which wasn’t previously provided by DJI.

articles.title: AMD heard you like powerful gaming portables — so here are new Strix Halo chips
articles.summary: AMD’s announcing two lower-end Ryzen AI Max Plus parts with full-fat graphics but fewer CPU cores, specifically aimed at gaming devices.
articles.body: AMD’s Strix Halo, aka “Ryzen AI Max,” is a hugely expensive chip that includes some of the most powerful integrated graphics ever made. Though AMD initially marketed it more to AI workloads with its tremendous complement of up to 128GB of RAM, it’s also inspired some unprecedented gaming designs — by far the most powerful handheld, the Framework Desktop, and this monster Asus tablet. But all those machines cost around $2,000, even before today’s global RAM shortages. Maybe that’ll change now that AMD’s announcing two lower-end Ryzen AI Max Plus parts with full-fat graphics but fewer CPU cores, specifically aimed at gaming devices. [Image: Screenshot They still have 40 graphics compute units for 60 teraflops, but the Ryzen AI Max Plus 392 has 12 cores rather than 16, and the Max Plus 388 has just eight CPU cores. “The reason we introduced the 392 and 388 chips is because those are the right products for gamers we’re bringing in,” AMD client chip boss Rahul Tikoo tells us in a press briefing. “Those two products were brought in because we had specific customer requests around gaming SKUs that we wanted to bring to market.” It’s not 100 percent clear whether new Strix Halo devices will be more affordable than the previous ones now that the price of RAM is skyrocketing, but take this as you will: Tikoo says that AI Max systems “can be over $1,000 to $1,500 price point” compared to vanilla Ryzen AI systems that typically start as low as $500. “$1,000 to $1,500” sure sounds like it could be less expensive than $2,000, but I don’t want to read too much into what could be an offhand remark. While we were impressed with the GPD Win 5 prototype, its rivals Ayaneo and OneXPlayer have announced Strix Halo handhelds as well.

articles.title: Nvidia announces RTX Spark as ‘the most efficient PC chip ever built’
articles.summary: Nvidia is announcing the RTX Spark, the first in a family of chips that will meet or beat the most powerful thin-and-light Windows machines ever, it claims.
articles.body: This fall, Nvidia will officially become a consumer PC chipmaker like Intel, AMD, Apple, and Qualcomm, putting a complete computing chip — not just graphics — into the very heart of laptops and mini-PCs. After many months of leaks, it’s finally announcing the RTX Spark, the first in a family of chips that will meet or beat the most powerful thin-and-light Windows machines ever, it claims. “This is the most efficient PC chip ever built,” says Nvidia senior director of product management Mark Aevermann — without sharing so much as a single statistic or chart to back that up. The RTX Spark is effectively the same GB10 chip that’s in the DGX Spark, the tiny “personal AI supercomputer” that Nvidia released last year, only now it’s a family of chips instead of just one. The flagship version appears to be spec-to-spec identical with 20 CPU cores, 6,144 GPU cores, and 128GB of LPDDR5X memory. [Image: Nvidia’s CEO holds up two RTX Spark laptops at Computex. But Nvidia says there’ll be lesser versions later, targeting lower prices, and with as little as 16GB of RAM. Like Apple and Qualcomm’s chips, this Nvidia chip is Arm-based silicon, meaning legacy Windows software made for Intel and AMD’s x86 processors needs to run through an emulation layer to work. That can mean lower performance. But Microsoft has now spent years getting Windows and its Prism emulator ready for Qualcomm and now Nvidia chips, and Nvidia claims its own graphics and AI chops will take the idea further than ever before. [Image: If these specs sound familiar, it’s because they’re the same as the DGX Spark AI mini-PC. With the power of the RTX Spark, Nvidia boasts, you can render a 90GB 3D scene, edit 12K resolution video, or play the graphically intensive Indiana Jones and the Great Circle at a smooth 100fps at 1440p resolution — all in a 14mm thick laptop without a power cord plugged in. [Image: Nvidia says RTX Spark laptops should have these features. And with up to 128GB of unified memory, tied with AMD’s previous gen Strix Halo parts, an RTX Spark laptop or desktop can also host 120-billion-parameter AI agents, something that Microsoft is seemingly excited about for Windows. At Microsoft’s Build conference this week, it’ll be showing off “new Windows security and containment primitives” that, along with Nvidia’s OpenShell runtime, “allows personal agents to run safely and under full user control.” Nvidia claims this adds up to “a new personal computing paradigm where AI is the UX” and “users no longer need to master complicated app UIs” because you’ll just talk to your PC instead of needing to use a mouse and keyboard. [Image: “Personal AI” for Windows. Nvidia suggested that, for example, a esports streamer could get their PC to automatically turn off their lights, mute their microphone, and change their broadcasting mode when they want to step away and grab dinner. A designer could use Adobe to automatically turn a sketch into a full image, render a 3D model of it, then create a AI video just by asking. A software developer can automatically monitor their GitHub project and autonomously fix QA issues, with the AI agent taking over the laptop’s keyboard and mouse cursor to do “repetitive and boring” tasks. Nvidia says that with the RTX Spark’s local AI chops, your data stays private and you won’t be burning through tokens to do AI things. I’m not convinced Nvidia has pieced together the Star Trek computer just yet, but it does seem like the company has a lot of partners on board. Almost every major laptop vendor is accounted for, with eight specific laptops already confirmed for this fall: [Image: Asus ProArt P14 and P16, Dell XPS 16, HP OmniBook X14 and Ultra 16, Lenovo Yoga Pro 9N, Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra, and MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI. One of those is from Microsoft, which is putting the Nvidia RTX Spark in a new laptop that Surface boss Andrew Hill tells us is “the most powerful thing we’ve ever made.” It’s called the Surface Laptop Ultra: [Image: Those machines are apparently just the start. Aevermann says Nvidia’s partners are already working on over 30 laptops and over 10 desktops, with Acer, Asus, Dell, Gigabyte, HP, MSI, and Lenovo all on board. “RTX Spark is going to be a family of products that are going to attack a lot of different price points,” Aevermann promises. “The overall market opportunity that we see is quite large.” [Image: And between Microsoft and Nvidia’s wrangling efforts, lots of Windows developers are also on board with Arm. The company points out that “Blender, DaVinci Resolve, Maxon Cinema4D, Maxon Redshift, Topaz Photo, CapCut, Cubase, Bitwig Studio, Affinity by Canva and more all run natively on Arm today, as do the audio, video, MIDI, and control peripherals they require.“ Adobe is on board, with special optimizations for Premiere and Photoshop that take advantage of Nvidia’s new chip. Even games with anti-cheat that thumbed their nose at Linux and the Steam Deck are now supporting Windows on Arm, too. Microsoft writes that Riot Games is now bringing both League of Legends and Valorant to Windows on Arm. Krafton is bringing PUBG, and Nvidia tells us it’s working with more developers who use Easy Anti-Cheat, BattlEye, and Denuvo. (Epic’s Fortnite already came to Windows on Arm last November after an announcement last March.) Aevermann says “all the top games will run on RTX Spark and provide a great experience.” That’s a pretty high bar to meet! Here are some more developers Nvidia says it’s working with: [Image: There are still many open questions, of course. Neither Nvidia nor Microsoft gave us a clear idea of how much these computers might cost, save that the first batch this fall is “targeting the more premium price points in the market.” On “all-day battery life,” Aevermann would only say that we should “expect it to be much better than anything you’ve seen before on RTX laptops” and that “you won’t need a charger” if you’re not pushing heavy workloads. The chip scales down to “low, low single-digit” wattage and goes as high as 80 watts, he says. The latter means they could theoretically drain bigger laptop batteries in around an hour at full bore. On performance, Nvidia didn’t have a single statistic or chart to share, and Aevermann wouldn’t answer questions about how the RTX Spark family stacks up to chips from Intel, AMD, Apple, and Qualcomm, saying Nvidia will have more to share closer to launch. But he does say that depending on the application, it has roughly the graphical power of an RTX 5070 mobile GPU, and that we should expect the CPU portion to be “competitive with anything else out there in the Windows space.” Nvidia also wouldn’t say whether these chips, made on the TSMC 3 process in partnership with MediaTek, are being manufactured in the US or abroad. That got a no comment. [Media: Nvidia also wouldn’t comment on whether it plans to offer Linux driver support for the RTX Spark, as it’s currently focused on Windows. It wouldn’t comment on putting the Spark in gaming handhelds, like AMD did with its powerful Strix Halo. But it did answer a question that no, the RTX Spark won’t be paired with additional discrete GPUs — which may limit its potential in desktops beyond the miniature ones, the same way Apple’s Mac Pro became limited when its Arm-based chips broke compatibility with discrete GPUs. Maybe it doesn’t matter that Nvidia isn’t sharing proof to back up its claims. Back in 2020, Apple didn’t share any proof when it announced Apple Silicon. But when the M1 arrived, it upended our concept of laptop performance overnight.

articles.title: Ford’s first ultra-cheap EV is called Fathom, a full-featured truck for $28,350
articles.summary: Fathom translates as “six feet deep,” which is probably where Ford would like to bury the Slate Truck.
articles.body: For nearly a year now, Ford has been teasing big things at low prices from its next generation of EVs, a “Model T moment” built atop a new platform assembled in an innovative way. Today, we know the name and price of the first product to take advantage of that supposed moment: a midsize electric truck called Fathom that starts at just $28,350. That’s not exactly great news for fans of the Slate Truck, the new electric upstart that’s leaning hard into its feature-free nature by painting itself as the ultimate DIY machine. Paint, though, is among the long line of modern niceties omitted to help the Slate Truck reach its starting price of $24,950. That first Slate also famously lacks things like power windows, a touchscreen, or even a basic stereo system. Ford’s Fathom, on the other hand, will be a fully featured vehicle, including integrated Apple Maps running on what’s called a “large, high-resolution touch screen.“ And, yes, both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay will be supported. [Media: Where the Slate seats two by default (an optional, $5,000 SUV kit expands that to five), the base Fathom aims to have greater interior volume than a Toyota RAV4. It’ll have an open bed out back and a frunk, too. The base Fathom will also include all the sensors needed to power Ford’s hands-free Blue Cruise system, though actually using that service will almost definitely come at extra cost. For reference, Blue Cruise currently costs an additional $2,495 as a one-time purchase, or $495 annually. How will Ford bring all these relative luxuries to a truck that costs just $3,400 more than the Slate? They’re taking the same approach as your friendly local furniture liquidator: volume, volume, volume. Cars, trucks, and SUVs built on Ford’s Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform will come together in a new way, with the vehicle effectively split into multiple, parallel assembly lines. The front, rear, and middle of the vehicle can all be assembled in parallel, then effectively stuck together at the end before being shipped off to your local dealer with a blue oval out front. Additionally, the construction of the vehicles themselves will be simplified, reducing both component and labor costs. High-volume manufacturing plus streamlined assembly will be key to Ford making the Fathom’s suggested retail price viable. However, it was never production capacity that slowed down Ford’s EV aspirations in the past. Lack of interest from buyers and dealers have stymied the company’s prior battery-powered efforts, resulting in billions in losses and the cancellation of the F-150 Lightning. Will a new focus and lower price mean more success? The Fathom’s starting cost is close to half that of the Lightning, a factor that surely has to help. Ford says the Fathom will enter production at the company’s updated Louisville Assembly Plant next year, with deliveries happening before the end of 2027. Pre-orders open early next year. The Slate Truck, meanwhile, hits the streets later this year, giving it a roughly 12-month head start in what hopefully won’t be a four-wheeled race to the bottom.

articles.title: Should you switch back to wired headphones? Here's why Kylie Jenner and other celebrities are doing so
articles.summary: Why are so many celebrities using wired headphones? It's not because your AirPods aren't secure.
articles.body:
If you're old like me (or an aging millennial, anyway), you may have noticed a weird tech trend lately – wired headphones are making a comeback. Everyone from Kylie Jenner and Hailey Bieber to Ariana Grande and Dua Lipa have been spotted carrying or using a pair. Last week, a viral X post pointing this out spawned a wave of users across X and Reddit to speculate that celebrities know something that we, the mere masses, don't: your wireless earbuds can be hacked.

But is there any truth to that claim? Fortunately, you probably don't need to toss your $250 AirPods in the trash. Here's what you need to know.

Hate being caught with a tinfoil hat on but there's a reason why celebs wear wired headphones and not AirPods/bluetooth. — Barbra Wyre Updates✨ (@BarbraWyre) October 7, 2026

Hate being caught with a tinfoil hat on but there's a reason why celebs wear wired headphones and not AirPods/bluetooth.

Barbra Wyre Updates✨ (@BarbraWyre) October 7, 2026

Can your wireless Bluetooth earbuds be hacked?

Technically, just about anything can be hacked if someone has enough time, patience and expensive equipment to do it. The chances of a random person putting in the effort to eavesdrop on the podcast you're listening to on your morning commute are pretty slim, though.

Bluetooth – the wireless protocol that your phone uses to connect to wireless earbuds – has its vulnerabilities like anything else, but it uses various security techniques , like encryption, to make it harder for hackers to exploit. You can avoid most problems by making sure you unpair your phone from old devices you don't use anymore and always keeping your phone updated. If you want to be extra safe, you can turn off Bluetooth on your phone or laptop when you aren't using it.

The truth is, most of us aren't targets for someone who might want to use Bluetooth as a hacking vector. You're much more likely to become the victim of a phishing scheme or ransomware attack.

Instead, politicians, business executives and others who might be targets for espionage are more likely to be the targets of a Bluetooth hack. Famously, former Vice President Kamala Harris told Stephen Colbert that she uses wired "earpods" because of information she was privy to in classified briefings during her time in the Senate. "Don't be on the train using your earpods and thinking somebody can't listen to your conversation," Harris said.

So what's with the wired headphones everywhere?

In the case of celebrities wearing wired earbuds, it's indeed a trend. Y2K nostalgia is very much in right now , and what's more Y2K than wired headphones? Harper's Bazaar has declared them the "coolest it-girl accessory." And they pair up nicely with retro tech like iPods, which are making a comeback , just like cassette tapes and vinyl records before them.

There's some practicality involved too. Wired headphones don't require charging, so you'll never have a battery die mid-song. And as ABC News contributor Mike Muse said in a September segment , the wires signal that the wearer is more "cool" and "grounded" in an increasingly digital world. Given the pace of change and anxiety over AI , it's not that surprising that some folks are opting for a more analogue look with their personal tech.

So don't feel like you need to ditch your wireless earbuds out of fear of some latent security issue. But if you want to stick with what's trendy, wired earbuds are definitely having a moment.

articles.title: Apple’s new Find My-compatible remote will also work with your old Apple TV
articles.summary: If you own any Apple TV 4K or Apple TV HD, you can upgrade to the new Siri Remote with Find My for $59.
articles.body: You don’t need to buy the new Apple TV 4K just to get the updated Siri Remote with Find My and a built-in speaker, as it works with every model released going back to the Apple TV HD and is available to buy standalone for $59. Previous Siri Remotes had a basic iOS feature to help you find your misplaced remote, but this is better, with one notable catch. Now the remote has Find My support, but if you want to see exactly how far away it is on your iPhone with details like “20 feet,” rather than simply “far” or “near,” you will need to have an iPhone Duo, iPhone Air, or any iPhone 17 or later. Those are the only models that include its new N1 networking chip with support for Bluetooth channel sounding, which enables AirTag-like precision tracking, but without requiring a UWB chip. > Find My support is available on the Siri Remote (2nd generation and later). Precision Finding works on the Siri Remote (4th generation) paired with iPhone Duo, iPhone Air or iPhone 17 or later (excluding iPhone 17e) running the latest iOS software; availability varies by region. As Stephen Robles points out in a post on Threads, the new remote’s backward compatibility means only a couple of features are limited to the new Apple TV 4K, including its built-in mic and surround sound with paired HomePod speakers. It will start shipping on November 13th, the same date as the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K.

articles.title: $15 gets you Psychonauts 2, the latest Like a Dragon game, and more
articles.summary: We’re highlighting deals on Humble Choice’s membership this month, as well as Borderlands 4, Valve’s Index, and preorders for Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey.

articles.title: Android is using AI to suss out scammers in Google Messages
articles.summary: Android is introducing new scam defense features that aim to make it easier for users to evade mobile fraud, including bolstered protection in Google Messages.
articles.body: Android is introducing new scam defense features that aim to make it easier for users to evade mobile fraud, including bolstered protection in Google Messages and additional safeguarding tools. Building on the Scam Detection feature in Google Messages, a new “enhanced protection” setting will be rolling out in the coming weeks that taps into cloud-based Gemini AI models to quickly evaluate a potential scammer’s intentions in conversations with an unrecognized sender. “Scammers often disguise their true motives behind slow-burn conversations,” Google said in its update announcement. “This secure cloud analysis augments and extends our existing on-device detection, allowing us to identify novel and sophisticated attacks, actively uncovering and stopping abusers who try to hide their tracks.” User data is encrypted during this AI analysis and “processed in a secure dedicated space” that Google (and anyone else besides the user) can’t access. The enhanced protection mode will be opt-in, and also uses on-device Gemini Nano AI to inspect real-time web signals in unfamiliar URLs sent to the user before they’re opened to determine if the links are malicious. Additional security features announced today include blocking apps from enabling call forwarding, and notifying the user when someone attempts to do so, along with automatically concealing sensitive information while screen-sharing in Chrome and Android WebView. The scam detection feature for chat notifications Google introduced on Pixel phones last year is also expanding to devices from Honor, Motorola, Oppo, OnePlus, Realme, Tecno, Vivo, Xiaomi, and more. Google says it plans to bring it to “hundreds of millions of additional users later this year.”

articles.title: As a TV enthusiast, I was hoping for more from the Apple TV 4K
articles.summary: The new Apple TV 4K streaming box has a very premium price tag and doesn’t add desired home theater features.
articles.body: It’s been four long years since the last Apple TV 4K was released, and in that time there have been lots of hopes and dreams for features in whatever comes next. A new chip, 4K/120Hz support, audio passthrough, a remote locator, better home control integration — the 2022 Apple TV 4K is a great box, but there’s still plenty of room for improvement. With the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K announced on Tuesday, some of those hopes were met, while others were unfortunately left out. Coloring the announcement is the device’s price. Apple eliminated the cheaper 64GB, Wi-Fi-only model, leaving just the 128GB, Wi-Fi and Ethernet model — and bumped up its price to $300. I repeat, $300 for a streaming device. It’s a hefty price when every other major streamer on the market is at least half the cost. There are new features I like about this year’s Apple TV 4K. More processing power is great — although my third generation is still running plenty fast — as is the Find My support for when the remote inevitably gets lost in the couch cushions or tangled up in blankets. Built-in far-field mics for talking to Siri are nice, too, provided you don’t stuff the box into a credenza like I do. The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K also adds a dedicated AV1 decoder, which allows for higher-quality streaming from apps that support it, such as Netflix, which is excellent. Any potential improvement to streaming content is a welcome one. My primary concern, though, is how the Apple TV 4K performs as an integral piece of my home theater. Apple added the ability to create a surround sound system by using its HomePod 2 and HomePod Mini 2 smart speakers in matching pairs for fronts and surrounds. For Apple ecosystem fans looking to build out a surround setup akin to Sonos or Bose, it’s an interesting idea (and I’m all for getting people into immersive sound in their home theaters). But as I expect is the same for many people interested in pricey streaming hardware, I already have a sound system — it’s an Atmos setup with a combination of SVS and Revel speakers. I’m not setting up my two HomePod 2s in my living room and spending another $300 on a pair of HomePod Mini 2s to replace my existing speakers. [Image: The Apple TV 4K pairs with up to four HomePods (such as the Mini 2 pictured here) for surround sound. What I, and many current users, have been hoping for from the Apple TV 4K for years is the addition of audio passthrough. This would allow my more expensive and capable audio/video receiver to decode the raw audio stream instead of the Apple TV using its Continuous Audio Connection, which can cause some playback issues. Additionally, it would have been nice to see Apple support 120fps output, especially for those who use Moonlight to stream games to it. That’s a feature that would have set the Apple TV 4K apart from all the other streamers, which top out at 60fps, and helped to justify the high price. Apple could have also used it to pivot more into TV gaming. (For movies, though, the 60fps limit is not a huge deal, as the box can be set to output 24fps, allowing a native 120Hz TV to just use 5:5 pulldown.) Other premium features that would set Apple’s streaming box apart and make home theater enthusiasts throw their money at it include an HDMI input for HDMI passthrough or a digital optical out. I understand leaving them out if it meant raising the price further. This box is already expensive enough. But it does leave the Apple TV 4K in an uncomfortable spot, pairing a high-end price with features that are largely matched elsewhere for much less. Are these high-end omissions a concern for the majority of people? Not really. But those people are going to look at the $300 price tag of the Apple TV 4K and then at Google, Roku, or Amazon streaming devices, which are all half that price or less. The Apple TV 4K is looked at as the premium streamer option, but the now extra premium price without some of the, admittedly niche, features gives me pause. Maybe the new Apple TV 4K will surprise me. I’ve certainly been looking forward to it for a while. I already appreciate the way Apple handles privacy, and if Apple adds features in coming months, maybe it could be worth it. But that $300 price? It might be better spent elsewhere in your home theater setup.

articles.title: A Broken iPhone Duo Could Cost Up to $1,499 to Repair
articles.summary: The iPhone Duo, Apple's first foldable, is already an incredibly expensive phone, rolling in at $1,999 to start. But, while the buy-in price is high, it's also going to be extremely expensive if it breaks.
articles.body:
The iPhone Duo , Apple's first foldable, is already an incredibly expensive phone, rolling in at $1,999 to start. While the buy-in price is high, it's also going to be extremely expensive if it breaks.

Ahead of the iPhone Duo's release next week, the foldable's repair costs were found by 9to5Mac , and they're staggering if you don't have AppleCare+. They range from damage on the glass back of the phone costing you $199 to inner screen damage costing $999 to repair. Apple will apparently also charge up to $1,499 to fix "other damage," though it's not clear what exactly that means.

All of these prices will be drastically lowered by having AppleCare+. Because the iPhone Duo is such an expensive and complicated device, anyone dropping the cash to buy one should seriously consider bundling AppleCare with it. I'd even go further and suggest picking up an iPhone Duo case on top of that.

As scary as these high repair prices look, Apple basically skipped the era of fragile foldables. Back when the first Samsung foldables were coming out, they were notoriously prone to damage, with displays that had gaps when folded, allowing particles of sand to get in there and wreak havoc on the inner screen. You could even peel the outer layer of the display off, a problem so bad that Samsung actually had to get around by putting out a statement telling people that the outer display layer was not a screen protector.

To Apple's credit, the iPhone Duo probably won't be quite as fragile as the foldables of yore, but it is still a phone with plenty of moving parts, which can always lead to unforseen damage. But we probably won't know exactly how durable it is until it actually makes its way into people's hands later this month. There's also a chance that the Duo's unique display aspect ratio will make it one of the first foldables that's actually good for gaming .

articles.title: The best feature of Apple’s HomeView might be its simplicity
articles.summary: If Apple’s first smart display finally gets my family to actually use my smart home, I’ll consider it a win.
articles.body: I’m just going to come right out and say it. I love the approach Apple has taken with the HomeView. I think it’s the shared, always-available household interface that my family might finally use. Is Apple’s first smart display my dream smart home dashboard? No. But is it the right product for Apple Home at this moment? Absolutely. A lot of initial reactions to the $299 HomeView (which looks like a giant Apple Watch on a flatter metallic HomePod Mini) ask why you would want it when you can do most of what it offers on your iPhone or iPad. And yes, its features replicate many of the things you already do on the devices you use all the time. But that’s kind of the point. HomeView gives you another interface for those things, but crucially one that is always powered, always unlocked, and always in the same spot in your home, making it easy to walk up to and interact with. I’ve tried using an iPad to control my smart home, run my family’s calendar, and be a shared device for controlling music. It wasn’t great. I’ll have to test HomeView, of course, but my initial impression is that this could be a much better solution for those use cases. [Image: My iPad in the wall experiment lasted several unsuccessful years. Most iPads are more expensive, have worse speakers, and do not like to be plugged in all the time (I present my sad, warped iPad Mini as tribute). An iPad can’t be a hub for your Apple Home; HomeView can. An iPad famously isn’t a good multiuser device, and controlling home devices on one requires it staying logged in to your personal iCloud account; HomeView offers Apple’s first crack at easy multiuser switching. Apple designed HomeView as a communal device that sits in a fixed place in the home. This means it’s always where you expect it to be, which matters when you want to adjust the thermostat or can’t find your phone and want to check your calendar. Not having a battery or detachable screen is a feature for me, because devices that do inevitably wander off and die under a couch cushion. And while many people are fine using their personal phones and tablets to interact with the digital world when at home, and don’t want yet another device with a screen on their countertop or wall, the millions of Echo Shows, Google Nest Hubs, Skylight Calendars, and the like in homes today are a good indicator that there’s interest in this type of interface. [Image: The HomeView’s footprint is smaller than that of most smart displays I’ve tested. As Apple’s uncharacteristically chaotic launch video shows, HomeView targets a new demographic for the company: busy, Apple-centric households. One feature I’m most interested in is HomeView’s role as a home video phone. Do you know how many times I’ve tried to call my daughter when I’m not home, and her phone is dead or on silent? Based on Apple’s video, if she’s home, my call can now ring on the HomeView. I’ve occasionally used the drop-in feature on Echo smart speakers to get her attention, further proof of the advantage of always-on home devices. [Image: [Image: I see HomeView as filling the awkward space where families don’t want phones at the dinner table or on the kitchen counter, but still want to check what time Zoey’s soccer game is or look up the origin of French toast (yeah, just kidding). This inevitably ends with one person pulling out their phone, which gives everyone else implicit permission to do the same. Smart displays and speakers from Amazon and Google already help with this to some extent, but Apple’s version comes without ads (see the Echo Show) and may have a longer lifespan (RIP Pixel Tablet). Siri AI’s much-hyped “personal context” capabilities, in which it can scan your text messages and emails and serve up relevant information to up to six members of your household, also give it an edge here. [Image: The HomeView has a variety of customizable faces. I asked Kaiann Drance, vice president of product marketing for home at Apple, why Apple chose now for its biggest smart home push yet. She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” she said. "As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in a natural way.”" - Lilian Rincon, Apple Siri AI made this possible because it’s “much more capable,” said Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI at Apple. She also pointed to its new conversational abilities. “It’s great because you can just ask it to change the temperature on your thermostat in a very natural way. As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in this natural way.” On why now, Rincon says the natural-language shift is the point where AI goes mainstream. “Because now it can be … my mother-in-law or the Gen Z who’s in college, both of them can use this in the way that they naturally speak and get what they want.” Siri AI in the home has another big advantage over the competition: It doesn’t say too much. Based on the demos I saw, and my time using Siri AI on the iPhone, when you ask it to do something, it does it without peppering you with follow-up questions. Rincon confirmed this is by design. “A lot of these assistants out there are always asking questions because they want more information,” she said. “For us, it isn’t about that. We’re there to get it done, take an action for you, show you what you need to get done, and then really get out of the way.” [Image: The Home control widget on the HomeView can show live views of security cameras. My first reaction to hearing about HomeView’s smart home features, which are basically just what the Apple Home app on your phone can do, was disappointment. I had hoped that, along with new hardware, Apple would bring more functionality and deeper Apple Intelligence integration to Apple Home to make the smart home smarter. I’m still waiting on that. On reflection, I’m okay with this — for now. Apple trying to make the smart home easier for everyone to use can only be a good thing. As always, the smart home’s most important goal is to come up with an easier way to turn on the lights. HomeView’s simplicity may put off hardcore home automation enthusiasts, but I’d argue it’s perfect for their long-suffering spouses. I’ve tried every version of physical smart home control interface in my home, and you know who hasn’t used any of them? My family. Because my family all have iPhones, and because the HomeView will always be there and will feel familiar, I can see them actually using it. That means I could set up a full Home Assistant instance and run a detailed dashboard on a tablet in my office, then feed the scenes and devices into Apple Home so my husband and daughter can just tap to control them on a HomeView in the kitchen. HomeView may not be the smart home computer I want Apple to make, but it is the smart home device Apple needed to make. It doesn’t have to run all the iPad apps or try to be a bigger version of my iPhone; it just needs to make the smart home accessible to everyone in the house. If Apple has pulled that off, it could be more valuable than any new smart home feature I’ve been wishing for. Photos by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

articles.title: As Apple becomes the first company to join Nvidia in $5 trillion club, here's the big 'iPhone message' from investors
articles.summary: Apple has become the second company after Nvidia to close with a market value above $5 trillion, underscoring investors’ continued faith in the iPhone
articles.body: Apple has become the second company after Nvidia to close with a market value above $5 trillion, underscoring investors’ continued faith in the iPhone maker despite the growing conversion over increasing hardware costs, AI competition and slowing growth. According to a report by Wall Street Journal, Apple ended trading a market capitalisation of about $5.005 trillion, making the first time the company has finished a trading session above the $5 trillion threshold. The milestone caps the tenure of former CEO Tim Cook, who oversaw a 13-fold increase in Apple’s market value during his 15 years at the helm. While, the rise of Nvidia has been fuelled by the AI boom and massive data centre sending, Apple’s ascent reflects something different: investor confidence in the resilience of its ecosystem and, most importantly, the willingness of iPhone users to continue paying more for Apple devices.The investor message: confidence despite cost pressureInvestors are so confident in Apple’s business that they have pushed up its shares even as big cost increases threaten profit margins. The cost of memory and storage chips inside iPhones, Macs and iPads has soared because data-center demand has caused shortages. Apple has responded by raising prices across its device lineup, including for older iPhone models that would typically get a price cut.In theory, that could hurt Apple, since buyers might wait longer to upgrade. Yet Apple shares have jumped 25% since the first wave of price increases.Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan said investors believe Apple’s customers will pay the higher prices, letting the company earn as much or more in total profit even if margins fall. He added that the new foldable iPhone Duo is likely to be popular and that the new Siri AI should prompt upgrades.Tim Cook’s recordCook’s act will be tough to follow. During his 15-year tenure as CEO, which ended Aug. 31, Apple’s market capitalization grew 13-fold. The company nearly quadrupled its annual iPhone sales. Its services business grew from $10 billion a year to more than $100 billion. The Apple Watch and AirPods, which he launched, together generate more than $30 billion a year. Apple also returned more than $1 trillion to shareholders through buybacks and dividends.Apple shares trade at a premium to the S&P 500 even though its revenue is growing more slowly than the index average. Analysts say that is because investors see the shares as safe and the business as predictable. A key to that has been limited capital spending, which boosts returns and lowers risk. That has been especially clear during the AI build-out, when big tech rivals have rushed to spend huge sums on data centers while Apple has stuck to making devices and selling high-margin services for them.AI remains the challengeAI has long been seen as Apple’s Achilles’ heel. The company failed to build its own frontier model and let Siri fall far behind rivals. Apple hopes the new Siri AI, built with Google’s help and released this fall, will change that. It still lags rival AI systems in key respects, but it is built directly into the iPhone, which many people already use. Apple also has access to more personal data, which could in theory power compelling features, though new AI agents show the technology is advancing faster than Apple can keep up.OpenAI threat and legal fightPerhaps the biggest threat is OpenAI, which is planning a family of AI-powered devices and has poached hundreds of Apple employees to drive its hardware strategy. Apple sued OpenAI in July, alleging it stole trade secrets. OpenAI has said it is “not aware of any evidence that this complaint has merit.” In a new filing Wednesday, it alleged that Apple poached one of its own employees, who took confidential files with him. Apple said it found no evidence supporting that allegation.AI could be where Ternus makes his mark, the Journal said. He could usher in a new era of innovation and growth, or Apple could finally lose its status as the company that defines how people interact with computers.You use AI every day. articles.title: World’s most valuable memory chip maker to US: Accept this 'China condition' if you want us to build factories in America
articles.summary: SK Hynix is reportedly seeking US approval to expand its China operations.
articles.body: SK Hynix is reportedly seeking US approval to expand its China operations. According to a report by the news agency Reuters, the South Korean memory chipmaker wants Washington’s permission to export additional US-made semiconductor manufacturing equipment to its Dalian facility in China. The report cited two people familiar with the matter, who said SK Hynix has made this a condition for funding its planned investment in American manufacturing.The report claims that the company’s US unit, Solidigm, is seeking an export licence to install equipment for producing NAND flash memory chips in unused space at the Chinese site. As per the report, the company is linking its plans for a new NAND factory in the US to its ability to increase production in China.The development comes as the Trump administration pushes foreign semiconductor companies to establish manufacturing facilities in America, while Washington continues to restrict China’s access to advanced chipmaking technology.Why SK Hynix wants US approval for its China facilitySolidigm wants to install additional equipment at SK Hynix’s Dalian facility to manufacture NAND flash memory chips. These chips power solid-state drives (SSDs), which are increasingly important for data centres supporting artificial intelligence (AI) and cloud computing workloads.The Dalian facility already uses semiconductor manufacturing equipment supplied by US companies, including Lam Research, Applied Materials and KLA. However, Solidigm needs additional authorisation to purchase and install more US-made equipment at the site.The report cited one person familiar with the matter, who said the company believes increasing production in China would help Solidigm finance a NAND manufacturing facility in the US. It would also help pave the way for expanding production capacity in America.In a statement to Reuters, SK Hynix said, "The installation of equipment for Mod B is being carried out in close consultation with and under authorisation from the US government."The company added, "No capacity expansion is being sought for the Dalian Mod B, which was completed in 2023."Solidigm declined to comment, while the US Department of Commerce did not respond to a request for comment.US export restrictions complicate SK Hynix’s plansThe request comes as Washington works to limit China’s access to semiconductor manufacturing technology. The US government has imposed export restrictions on chipmaking equipment to slow Beijing’s development of advanced semiconductors used in AI and military applications.Last year, the US Department of Commerce revoked authorisations that had allowed SK Hynix and Samsung to obtain US equipment for their Chinese factories without applying for individual licences. The department described the previous arrangements as a "Biden-era loophole."Instead, the government said it would issue export licences allowing the companies to operate their existing Chinese facilities, while signalling that it did not expect to approve applications for capacity expansion or technology upgrades.In December 2025, the department issued a licence for SK Hynix’s Dalian plant for 2026 but restricted the amount of equipment that could be exported. One source said the company has not yet been approved for more US-made equipment and technology for 2027.Mod B is a manufacturing facility in Dalian, built in 2023. Even after the memory market went into the doldrums, the equipment was not installed.SK Hynix’s plans for a US factoryThe proposed American NAND factory is part of SK Hynix’s broader efforts to expand its manufacturing presence in the US. Reuters reported last month that Solidigm was considering building a NAND flash memory factory in the country.The company is also reportedly in talks with Intel to lease part of its planned chipmaking facility in Ohio. Separately, SK Hynix has broken ground on an advanced packaging plant in Indiana focused on high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which is used in AI systems.Building semiconductor fabrication plants, commonly called fabs, requires billions of dollars and can take several years. Another source said that Solidigm is also weighing an initial public offering (IPO) as early as next year, which could provide additional funding for its US factory plans.NAND memory market drives expansion plansSK Hynix’s request comes after the NAND market has recovered from a previous downturn and struggled with supply constraints. Walt Coon, memory industry expert at TechInsights, said NAND pricing has surged sevenfold since mid-2023 and the market is likely to remain tight over the next few years.The company is one of the two leading global suppliers of NAND flash memory, alongside Samsung Electronics. However, China's YMTC moved up to third place in the second quarter of 2026, according to Counterpoint Research.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Ledger’s new hardware wallet is an Android phone without the phone
articles.summary: The Ledger Atom is a data-only Android device designed to work alongside your phone as a hardware wallet signer.
articles.body: Ledger has announced its latest crypto-centric hardware effort, the Android-based Atom, a device that resembles a phone but is instead designed to be used alongside one. It arrives at a tricky time for Ledger, which has been forced to cease sales of some of its hardware across southeast Asia following hardware tampering in its supply chain, which has reportedly seen over $86 million worth of crypto stolen from across some users’ accounts. While Ledger’s previous hardware wallet signers have been compact devices, running custom software and often with E Ink displays, the Atom is the spitting image of a regular Android smartphone. In fact it essentially is an Android phone, except for the fact that its eSIM capabilities have been limited to data-only, with no support for texting or calls. The Atom runs on both Android OS and Ledger OS, which sits on its own secure element chip, allowing you to move into a secure environment for tasks like crypto transactions. Two Atom users can also send encrypted messages to one another using regular Android messaging apps, with the messages decrypted within Ledger OS on the recipient’s device. Ledger has designed the device with AI agents in mind, including a partnership with OpenClaw, designed so that agents can handle financial tasks without getting full access to digital wallets, with physical approval required to complete transactions. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Ledger says that the Atom is “not designed to replace your phone.” The company’s head of PR, Phillip Costigan, told me that Ledger recognized it was unlikely to be able to produce a device capable of competing with top Android handsets on camera and other specs, and so didn’t try to. The Atom is in fact intentionally limited in some respects: the 6.77-inch OLED display is only 60Hz, it runs on a Qualcomm Dragonwing chip rather than Snapdragon, and it only has a single rear camera and a 4,000mAh battery. Still, it will receive five years of Android OS updates, and at least seven years of support for spare parts, including a user-replaceable battery. It also has a physical privacy switch, which cuts power to the camera and microphone “at a circuit level.” The launch couldn’t come at a worse time for Ledger. The company has confirmed reports that at least one of its hardware signers was sold by a reseller with “an unauthorized hardware implant,” which read users’ 24-word recovery phrases and transmitted them elsewhere using an eSIM. The discovery has forced Ledger to pause sales across southeast Asia, and at German retailer MediaMarkt. Reports suggest that over $86 million worth of crypto may have been stolen from across affected users, though Ledger hasn’t confirmed the scale of the losses. That would be enough to give anyone pause before buying new Ledger hardware, at least from a third-party seller. Still, the company says that the Atom has been designed with physical anti-tampering measures, which it claims would have blocked the screen reader implants involved in the recent incident: > Core protection: A protective enclosure surrounds the Secure Element, MCU, and FPGA, and it is designed to detect any attempt to drill into or open this area. > Display and back cover detection: Ledger Atom detects when the display or back cover is removed. The back cover is paired with the device, so it cannot be swapped with a cover from another Ledger Atom. > Tamper-evident packaging: Ledger Atom’s packaging is designed to show whether it has been opened before it reaches you. The Atom will be available from summer 2027. Reservations are open now, with a refundable $100 deposit to secure a Founder’s Edition device for $849. After the launch, the price will rise to $899.

articles.title: Amazon’s always-listening Bee wearable can now help you buy stuff
articles.summary: The new Alexa and Amazon integrations require a subscription. Plus, a magnetic version for your phone is coming ‘soon.’
articles.body: Last year, Amazon bought Bee, a relatively unknown startup with a $50 always-listening AI wearable that summarized every conversation you had. Today, the e-commerce giant is announcing two new Bee devices — and a new subscription to go with them. First is the $74.99 Bee Frontier, an updated version of the original Bee device. And coming soon is the $99.99 Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-shaped gadget that snaps magnetically onto the back of a smartphone. Both devices are framed as gadgets to help you stay present in the moment. They listen to your daily conversations and then provide summaries, transcripts, insights, and to-dos based on what happens throughout the day. Conceptually, they’re similar to other AI note-taking gadgets like Plaud NotePin and Limitless AI. Users can also integrate Bee devices with services like Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, Apple HealthKit, and photos. Doing so lets Bee’s AI take some actions on your behalf, like drafting emails or sending calendar invites based on your conversations. [Image: Both the Eclipse (left) and Frontier (right) feature recording indicator lights. The main difference between the two products is form factor. The Bee Frontier can be worn as a Fitbit-like band on the wrist or as a clip-on pin. It’s been slightly redesigned from the prior model so that the recording button is more prominent, and it’s now available in three colors. Like the previous version, it has dual microphones, a recording indicator light, and roughly seven days of battery life on a single charge. It also has an IP67 water resistance rating. Meanwhile, the Eclipse is meant as a non-wearable alternative and is envisioned for more professional use cases. Its larger size allows for a bigger battery, getting 21 days on a single charge. It, too, has a recording indicator light. While these devices are free to use, Amazon is also introducing a Bee Pro subscription for $11.99 a month. The free tier gets users conversation summaries, recaps, and 14 days of memory. The subscription gets users “unlimited” summaries, suggested to-dos, daily memories, a personal chat assistant, conversation templates, third-party app integrations, and a desktop app. But the big marquee feature for the subscription is Amazon and Alexa Plus compatibility. The Amazon integration is opt-in, and doing so will enable the device to surface shopping suggestions based on your conversations. For example, if your spouse asks you to buy cat litter, you might see a product card reminding you of that on your Amazon homepage or an Amazon button linking out to the product in the Bee mobile app. The Alexa Plus integration is meant to be a hands-free way to access your various Bee summaries and insights. It’s an interesting time for Amazon to introduce these products, given the recent backlash against so-called surveillance tech. On that front, Amazon told The Verge in a press briefing that Bee devices encrypt transcripts, summaries, and to-dos via its “Private Compute” security architecture and don’t store audio recordings. Bee devices can also be programmed to automatically stop recording if no sound is detected after a certain period of time. As for whether transcripts are attributable, that depends. Upon setup, Bee’s AI is trained on the individual user’s voice. All other speakers are not automatically identified unless you ask them to also allow Bee’s AI to train on their voice. Whether that’s enough to assuage any privacy concerns, well, that depends on your definition of a recording. The Bee Frontier is available starting today for $74.99 in black, green, and lavender. The Eclipse is “coming soon” for $99.99 and is available in black, pink, yellow, and silver.

articles.title: Amazon's Bee launches two new personal AI devices, starting at $75 | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Amazon-owned Bee has launched its first new AI devices since its acquisition, including an updated wearable and a credit-card-sized recorder that attaches to smartphones. The devices can summarize conversations, create to-do lists, and integrate with Alexa and Amazon shopping, with prices starting at $74.99.
articles.body:
Amazon’s personal AI wearable maker, Bee , is announcing its first new products since being acquired by the retail giant last year . The tech company on Thursday introduced the Bee Frontier, the next generation of its device that can be worn on the wrist or pinned to clothes, along with Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of your smartphone.

The latter puts Bee into more direct competition with AI devices like the Plaud Note or Pocket, but at a lower price point — the Bee Frontier is $74.99, compared with $159 for the Plaud Note (or $189 for the Note Pro), or $129 for the Pocket AI device .

The Bee Frontier will come in Onyx, Lavender, and Sage, while the $99.99 Bee Eclipse will be offered in Silver, Midnight, Honey, and Blush.

Like the original Bee, the idea with the new devices is to leverage AI to take notes from your everyday conversations, allowing you to remember the important things that were said, and then turn those into actionable to-dos, summaries, and insights.

For instance, if you discussed making plans with friends, the Bee would remember the date and time you agreed on, then create a calendar invite. You could also use the Bee to take lecture notes in class, or to jot down the care plan you discussed with a doctor, among other things.

All Bee devices can create conversation summaries and recaps for free, and offer 14 days of memory. With an $11.99 per month Bee Pro subscription, users receive unlimited conversation summaries and integrations with Amazon.com, Alexa+, and third-party applications. Pro users also get suggested to-dos, daily memories, a personal chat assistant, and conversation templates.

To make all this possible, Bee devices use a private computing security architecture, which doesn’t store the raw audio from your conversations. Instead, audio is processed in real time and then deleted. Transcripts of the conversation are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls, which means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you manually and intentionally share them.

In addition, you can opt to connect the Bee to Alexa, allowing your Echo device to use its ability to identify your voice, a feature called Voice ID, to recognize when you’re speaking. It can then record your conversations to provide Bee’s insights. (This aspect of Bee is optional, and Amazon notes you can delete transcripts and summaries at any time.)

With its new connections to Amazon.com and Alexa, Bee users can make purchases from Amazon or ask Alexa for their Bee insights, summaries, or to-dos hands-free.

Bee also works with your existing productivity software, like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Microsoft Outlook, so it can draft emails, set up meetings, surface action items, and more.

Plus, you can upload photos to Bee or connect it with Apple’s HealthKit to add a picture of your overall wellness to be integrated into your provided insights.

The Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse both have just one button that turns the device off and on, and include an indicator light when it’s summarizing a conversation. The Frontier also offers IP67 water resistance, up to seven days of battery life, USB-C charging, and dual microphones with advanced noise filtering.

All Bee devices come with a companion mobile app, which has also been newly redesigned, plus a new desktop app.

The Bee Frontier is available now on Amazon, and the Eclipse will be available soon thereafter.

articles.title: Quick question: Who exactly is iPhone Handoff for?
articles.summary: Apple announced a new way to use one phone number across two iPhones, no eSIM transfer required. But who’s actually going to use it?
articles.body: Last month, Apple announced a feature called iPhone Handoff. Not to be confused with that Handoff; this is a new one. iPhone Handoff allows you to keep your number active on two iPhones at the same time so you can easily switch between them. According to Apple’s support website, you pick one phone as your main phone and set up Handoff on the other as your secondary phone. When you unlock one of them, your number becomes active on that phone — that’s where you’ll get calls, and that device will be used for Find My. The idea is that your secondary phone will be something you pick up on weekends, for example, with apps and settings configured to your needs, and Handoff means you can use it with your existing phone number. Apple is pitching it as a totally seamless way to use your number on two phones, but that convenience comes at a cost. T-Mobile is the first US carrier to support the feature, and it’s an extra $5 on your monthly phone bill to use it. Verizon is also planning to support Handoff by the end of the year. If you’re on AT&T you’re out of luck, it seems. As someone who uses a lot of different phones, this all sounds handy. But the more I considered how it would actually work, the more I wondered: Who is this feature really for? Why not just switch your eSIM? As I read up on it, the wilder it seemed. And so I present my short list of potential iPhone Handoff users, ranked from least to most speculative. You want to live the Duo lifestyle but you don’t want to give up your slab phone Given that Apple announced Handoff when it unveiled the Duo, this is likely a scenario that Cupertino had in mind. You want the benefits of a medium phone that turns into a giant phone, but you also want to use your regular iPhone sometimes. Seems reasonable, I guess. Photo quality could be one motivator here since the Duo comes with downgraded camera hardware. Or maybe you just don’t want to carry the heavier, bulkier Duo on weekends. Maybe you just like gadgets and you want to switch between phones on a whim. The heart wants what the heart wants! [Image: If you want a Duo but don’t want to carry this chunk around all the time, maybe iPhone Handoff is for you. You have a work phone and a personal phone I don’t know a lot of people who live the dual work/personal phone lifestyle, and I haven’t had a work phone since my BlackBerry Curve, rest its soul. But this could be a genuinely nice feature for someone who needs to keep two phones around but doesn’t want two phone numbers. But that’s the key — if your work phone already has a phone number through an account that’s managed by your employer, then Handoff as it works now isn’t an option. T-Mobile specifies that the secondary iPhone you’re using with Handoff “should not have any other service attached to it,” and that it can’t be used with a T-Mobile business account at launch. Kinda seems like a niche use case. You have a small, fun iPhone that can’t hack it as your main phone Do I have a personal bias here? Yes. But I don’t think I’m totally alone. Maybe you love your iPhone Air or you’re holding on to an iPhone Mini for dear life, neither of which has great battery life. So maybe Handoff lets you get a newer phone with better battery and cameras while still holding on to the smaller phone to use on lighter days or weekends. Could I set up my 13 Mini as a more minimalist phone without social media and switch back to it when I want to take a break? Totally. Do I have the self-discipline to actually do that on a regular basis? Uh, I plead the Fifth. You work at Apple Sometimes the ideas that come out of Cupertino seem to solve problems only an Apple employee could have. This feels like one of them. Do you read a lot of PDFs in business class? Do you have the disposable income to keep another iPhone around rather than trading it in to offset the cost of a $2,000 phone? Do you insist on elegant solutions even when they create unneeded complexity? Congratulations, you probably work for Apple. But… why? Realistically, I think very few people will want or need Handoff, and that’s fine. Did Apple engineers with multiple iPhones invent a feature to make their own lives easier? Maybe! They get to do that! But I have a theory for the rest of us who like the idea of a secondary iPhone and don’t work in a big glass circle: Try a cellular Apple Watch and see if that doesn’t do the trick. An always-connected smartwatch remains the best minimalist phone, and I grow more convinced of this every year. You get access to messages, calling, music, and navigation. It already shares your phone number. And you can customize what notifications you’ll get so that it doesn’t bother you with Instagram pings if that’s the freedom you’re looking for. But if you truly need two phones and you don’t want to pay your carrier for the privilege of having your line active on both, I have more good news: Swapping eSIMs between iPhones is reliable and free, and it only ruins your life if you’re a professional phone user.

articles.title: Microsoft says Windows 11 is now ‘more responsive’ and runs better on 8GB of RAM
articles.summary: A lot of the speed improvements are thanks to smarter ways to manage memory and PC resources.
articles.body: Earlier this year Microsoft laid out a plan to fix Windows 11, with a focus on performance, reliability, and the overall OS experience. After months of fixes, Microsoft now says the “result is a Windows experience that’s up to 20 percent more responsive.” Microsoft has made improvements to Start, File Explorer, Search, Edge, and other parts of Windows 11 to make it feel faster and more responsive. “A big part of that work is making smarter use of memory and system resources,” says Navjot Virk, corporate vice president of Windows experiences at Microsoft. “We’ve improved memory management and efficiency across Windows to help keep more of your PC’s resources focused on what you’re actively doing.” The improvements to memory management now make a “meaningful difference” on PCs with just 8GB of RAM. “Windows can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage,” says Virk. “For example, on PCs with 8GB of memory or less, Widgets load only when you open them, making more than 200 MB of memory available for your apps and other work.” Microsoft has also made Windows Update less disruptive, cleaned up the Widgets section, and finally allowed the taskbar to be repositioned to the sides or top of a display. Windows Hello sign-in has also been sped up, and Bluetooth pairing is more reliable, “including an AirPods pairing experience that’s up to 15 seconds faster.” The next big step is a new Windows Search experience that’s a lot faster and more capable. I got to try it out last week and I think it’s one of the best new additions to Windows 11 this year. It’s currently available for Windows Insiders, and Microsoft says it will “roll out more broadly later this year.”

articles.summary: Microsoft has redesigned its Photos app for Windows 11, combining photos and videos from your PC, OneDrive, and iCloud into a single space.
articles.body: Microsoft has redesigned its Photos app for Windows 11, overhauling the editor and image viewer, and combining photos and videos from your PC, OneDrive, and iCloud into a single space. The new combined gallery experience aims to make it easier to manage and view your photos without jumping between apps or devices, while also improving app launch and scrolling performance in Photos. To combine your galleries in the Windows 11 Photos app, you’ll need to turn on Camera Backup in the OneDrive mobile app on iOS or Android, and follow Apple’s guide to set up iCloud for Windows. Once combined in the Windows 11 Photos app, you can browse by date, organize and share albums, search for specific photos via descriptions or by the people featured in them, and more. You can browse files online or offline, and Microsoft says photos will be available on your device “even when you’re not connected.” The new Photos editor has been “rebuilt from the ground up,” according to Microsoft, launching 25 percent faster and arranging tools into four categories: Crop, Enhance, Repair, and Stylize. The Photos app now also preserves HDR quality during editing processes and allows you to edit and save HEIC and WebP images without altering their original format. [Image: Here’s an example of the tools you’ll find under the new “Crop” category. Lastly, the viewer has been given a cleaner layout and performance enhancements, launching 15 percent faster and opening HEIC images up to 30 percent faster, according to Microsoft’s announcement. Media type support has also expanded to SVG files. These new Photos experiences are rolling out today as an update for Windows Insiders on Windows 11, with Microsoft expecting a full launch for all Windows 11 users later this year.
